messages.content: I want to characterize when heterogeneous treatment effects remain partially identifiable with weak instruments and bounded exclusion violations in observational healthcare.

The aim is to determine what can still be learned about variation in treatment effects when an instrument offers limited identifying information and the exclusion restriction is allowed to fail within a bound. Partial identification means the available information may restrict an effect to a set of possible values without determining a single value. The characterization needs to say when those restrictions are informative for the heterogeneous effects of interest, not simply assume that having an instrument makes them informative.
So this is not necessarily a point-identification problem?

Right. A single identified value is not required. The central question is which effect values remain compatible with the observational information and the stated restrictions on instrument strength and exclusion violations. Depending on those restrictions, the answer may be a nontrivial set, or the instrument may add little to what could be said without it.
What does heterogeneous add to the question?

It means the target concerns variation in treatment effects, rather than only one overall effect. Any identification claim needs to be clear about which heterogeneous effects it covers. A bound for an overall effect would not, by itself, establish the same bound for each effect in a heterogeneous target.
And the instrument is weak, not assumed to be useless?

Exactly. Weakness describes limited identifying leverage; it does not, on its own, say that the instrument conveys no information. The issue is whether the information it does convey, together with a bound on exclusion violations, meaningfully restricts the heterogeneous effects. That answer can depend on the instrument-strength and exclusion-violation classes under consideration.
How should I interpret a bounded exclusion violation here?

It permits departures from exact exclusion, but limits how large those departures may be under the stated restriction. That is different from treating exclusion as exact, and also different from allowing unrestricted violations. The bound may preserve some identifying information, but it cannot be presumed to do so in every case.
I also need at least 95% confidence-set coverage uniformly over the specified instrument-strength and exclusion-violation classes. What is the force of uniformly?

The coverage requirement must hold across the specified classes, including the configurations within them that are difficult for inference. It is not enough to obtain at least 95% coverage at a convenient fixed configuration while falling below that level at another allowed strength or violation. The precise target of the confidence set must be stated clearly so that the coverage claim has an unambiguous meaning.
Could I describe that as 95% coverage on average across the classes?

No. An average could conceal undercoverage for some allowed configurations. Your requirement is at least 95% confidence-set coverage uniformly over the specified instrument-strength and exclusion-violation classes. It calls for a guarantee throughout those classes, not an average over them.
Does the coverage requirement establish that the identification bounds are informative?

No. Coverage is an inferential property of the confidence set; informativeness concerns how much the identification restrictions narrow the possible effects. A confidence set can meet its coverage requirement even when the underlying identification bounds are wide. Conversely, a narrow proposed bound does not establish that inference around it has the required uniform coverage.
What would it mean to establish sharp identification bounds?

The bounds must capture the full range of effect values compatible with the stated information and restrictions, without leaving out compatible values or retaining avoidable looseness at the extremes. In that sense, sharpness is about the identification claim itself. It is not a claim that a sample-based confidence set must be as narrow as the identification bounds.
The other requirement is to characterize when those bounds improve upon bounds without instruments. Is any improvement automatic?

No. The comparison has to be made for the same heterogeneous-effect target against bounds obtained without instruments. Weak instrumental information and permitted exclusion violations may, in some circumstances, narrow the range of compatible values; in others, they may not tighten its endpoints. The goal is to characterize when improvement occurs, not to claim that it always does.
If the instrument rules out some possibilities, does that necessarily mean the bounds improve?

Not necessarily. Ruling out possible values can make an identified set smaller without moving the endpoints of its reported bounds. To claim an improvement in bounds, the comparison needs to show that the relevant bound actually tightens relative to the bounds without instruments. It also matters that both sides of the comparison use the same target and clearly stated restrictions.
Could stronger instrument information offset a larger allowed exclusion violation?

That is the kind of relationship the characterization can examine, but the goal alone supplies no threshold or trade-off formula. More identifying information from an instrument and more latitude for exclusion violations pull in different directions. Whether their combination gives sharper or more informative bounds must follow from the specified classes and restrictions, rather than from a general slogan.
How should the observational healthcare setting figure into the statement?

It identifies the setting in which the treatment effects, instrumental information, and exclusion concerns arise. The statement should remain about heterogeneous treatment effects in observational healthcare, while avoiding claims about particular treatments, patients, instruments, or datasets that have not been specified.
I want to avoid conflating a confidence set with an identified set. Can you make the distinction explicit?

An identified set describes which heterogeneous-effect values are compatible with the observational information and imposed restrictions. A confidence set is a statistical procedure's output when those quantities must be inferred from data; its coverage concerns how reliably it contains its designated target. Sharp identification bounds and uniformly valid confidence-set coverage are therefore separate requirements, even though both concern the same substantive effects.
Does the goal say whether coverage should be simultaneous across every heterogeneous effect?

It does not specify that detail. Because heterogeneous effects can be indexed in different ways, the coverage target would need to be defined before claiming a particular guarantee. If a simultaneous guarantee is intended, coverage for each effect considered separately would not automatically establish it. What is explicit here is the threshold—at least 95%—and uniformity over the specified instrument-strength and exclusion-violation classes.
Then what is the full task, stated without implying any results have already been obtained?

Characterize when heterogeneous treatment effects in observational healthcare remain partially identifiable under weak instruments and bounded exclusion violations. Establish sharp identification bounds and determine when they improve upon bounds without instruments. Alongside that identification analysis, provide confidence sets with at least 95% coverage uniformly over the specified instrument-strength and exclusion-violation classes. None of those requested properties should be treated as established in advance.
Can we turn that goal into a concrete proposal without implying the bounds or coverage result have already been established?

Yes. The proposal is to derive sharp linear-programming (LP) bounds for stratified treatment effects under bounded exclusion violations, compare their widths with bounds obtained without instruments, and construct confidence sets by inverting uniformly valid 95% weak-IV-robust moment tests. Each part is work to be done: formulating and establishing the bounds, making the no-IV comparison, and demonstrating the stated coverage property.
What does “stratified-effect” commit us to here?

It keeps the heterogeneous-effect target at the level of specified strata rather than silently replacing it with one overall treatment effect. The proposal does not itself define those strata or identify a particular healthcare population. Once the targets are specified, each bound and comparison needs to refer to the same stratified effect.
Why use linear programming for the identification bounds?

The proposed LP approach is to express the information and restrictions defining the admissible possibilities as constraints, then minimize and maximize the stratified effect over those possibilities. Those extrema would supply lower and upper bounds. To justify calling them LP bounds, the formulation must actually represent the relevant objective and constraints in a form suitable for linear programming; the label alone does not establish that.
Where do bounded exclusion violations enter that optimization?

They enter as restrictions on which possibilities are admissible. Exact exclusion would rule out any violation, while an unrestricted violation would provide no such limit. Here the proposal is to allow violations within the specified bound and derive the stratified-effect bounds under that allowance. No numerical violation limit has been specified, so the proposal should not presume one.
Is it enough to obtain an LP solution and call its endpoints sharp?

No. Sharpness requires showing that the optimization captures all the possibilities permitted by the stated observational information and restrictions, and that its resulting endpoints cannot be tightened while retaining all compatible possibilities. An LP can be solved accurately yet give nonsharp identification bounds if its representation leaves out admissible cases or relaxes a restriction unnecessarily.
So both directions of the representation matter?

They do. Every possibility admitted by the intended model needs to be represented in the optimization, and every possibility counted by the optimization needs to satisfy the intended restrictions. Establishing that correspondence is part of deriving sharp bounds, rather than a consequence of merely writing down constraints.
How does instrument weakness affect the LP part?

The instrument-based restrictions may provide limited leverage when the instrument is weak. The LP bounds should reflect whatever restrictions remain under the specified instrument-strength and exclusion-violation classes, without assuming that weak instruments either identify a single effect or provide no information at all. Whether they narrow a stratified effect's bounds is something to determine, not to build into the conclusion.
And what exactly are the no-IV widths for comparison?

They are the widths of the bounds for the same stratified-effect targets when instrument-based identifying information is not used. A meaningful comparison holds the target and the other applicable information fixed, so a change in width can be attributed to the instrument-based restrictions rather than to changing the question being asked.
Should I compare only the numerical widths, or also the endpoints?

The proposal explicitly calls for comparing no-IV widths, so width is an essential comparison. Examining the lower and upper endpoints can also clarify what is happening: two bounds can have different endpoints yet the same width. If the claim is that an IV-based bound improves on a no-IV bound by narrowing it, the relevant width must actually decrease.
Could a weak instrument still lead to a narrower bound?

Possibly. Weakness does not logically imply that the instrument-based restrictions are redundant. But a narrower bound is not guaranteed, particularly when bounded exclusion violations also permit additional possibilities. The proposed comparison is meant to characterize when the LP bounds are tighter than their no-IV counterparts and when they are not.
Would a strict improvement mean a strict reduction in width for every stratum?

That would be a stronger claim than simply finding an improvement for a specified stratified effect. The comparison should state which stratified effects have strictly narrower bounds, which do not, and what conditions support each conclusion. The proposal supplies no result saying that every stratum improves.
Suppose an instrument-based restriction changes neither endpoint. How would we describe that?

For that target, the reported bounds would not improve over the no-IV bounds. The restriction could still be part of the formulation, but its presence alone would not justify claiming tighter bounds. The comparison should be about what the restrictions accomplish for the specified stratified-effect bounds.
Does LP sharpness solve the confidence-set problem too?

No. LP sharpness concerns the population identification bounds under the stated restrictions. A confidence set must also account for statistical uncertainty, and weak instruments can make inference difficult even when the population optimization is well defined. That is why the proposal separately calls for inverting weak-IV-robust moment tests.
What does inverting those tests mean in this context?

Conceptually, consider candidate values for a stratified effect, test the corresponding hypotheses using moment restrictions, and retain values that the test does not reject. The retained values form a confidence set. The test and its inversion must accommodate the bounded exclusion violations and whatever additional quantities the hypotheses leave unspecified; merely labeling a test weak-IV-robust would not establish validity.
Why specifically require weak-IV-robust moment tests?

Because the inference requirement includes instrument-strength classes in which conventional reasoning that depends on a strong instrument may not be reliable. The proposed tests must retain their claimed validity across the specified classes, including weak-instrument configurations, rather than relying on a coverage argument that works only when instrument strength is comfortably high.
How does the 95% requirement translate into a condition on the tests?

For an appropriately defined null and confidence-set target, inversion of tests with a uniformly controlled false-rejection probability of at most 5% can yield at least 95% coverage. The key qualification is uniformity: the required control must hold over the specified instrument-strength and exclusion-violation classes, not merely at a selected configuration.
Does calling the tests “95%” by itself guarantee that uniformity?

No. A nominal 95% label does not prove uniform coverage. The proposal calls for uniformly valid 95% weak-IV-robust moment tests; demonstrating that their error control holds throughout the specified classes is a substantive part of meeting the goal.
What if the bounded exclusion violation is handled in the LP but ignored in the test?

Then the identification and inference steps would be based on different restrictions. The proposed confidence procedure needs to respect the same permitted exclusion violations relevant to its target. Otherwise, a coverage statement over the specified exclusion-violation classes would not follow just from the sharpness of the LP bounds.
Should I say that inversion covers the whole identified set with probability at least 95%?

Only if that is the confidence target and the tests are calibrated to establish that particular guarantee. Inverting tests for individual candidate effect values does not, by itself, establish simultaneous coverage of every value in an identified set. The proposal should define what its confidence set is required to cover and prove at least 95% uniform coverage for that target.
Is uniform coverage across the instrument and violation classes the same as simultaneous coverage across all strata?

No. Uniformity over the specified instrument-strength and exclusion-violation classes concerns how the procedure performs across allowed configurations. Simultaneous coverage across multiple stratified effects is a distinct requirement. The proposal does not specify that latter guarantee, so it should not be claimed without defining and establishing it.
Can a confidence set be wide even if the IV-based LP bound is narrower than its no-IV counterpart?

Yes. A population-level improvement in identification bounds and the precision of a confidence set are different matters. The no-IV width comparison asks whether instrument information tightens the identification bound. The test inversion asks whether uncertainty is handled with the required coverage, including when the instrument is weak. Neither result automatically supplies the other.
How would you state the proposed workflow in one careful passage?

For each specified stratified treatment effect, formulate the admissible possibilities under the observational information and bounded exclusion violations, and derive sharp lower and upper bounds through an LP formulation. Compare the width of each resulting bound with the corresponding no-IV bound to characterize when instrument information provides a strict improvement. Then invert weak-IV-robust moment tests to form confidence sets, establishing at least 95% coverage uniformly over the specified instrument-strength and exclusion-violation classes. This describes what the analysis is intended to establish, not results already obtained.
At what exclusion-risk slack does a ≤5-point physician-preference first stage stop narrowing comorbidity-specific 30-day readmission bounds versus no-IV?

That is the threshold to determine, not a threshold we can read off from the question alone. For each specified comorbidity stratum, we would compare the width of its instrument-based 30-day readmission bound at a given exclusion-risk slack with the width of the corresponding no-IV bound. The instrument stops narrowing that bound where the widths cease to show a strict improvement. No numerical slack value or bound widths have been supplied.
So the ≤5-point first stage does not itself tell us where the cutoff is?

Correct. It describes the physician-preference first-stage condition in the question, but does not determine how much identifying information survives a given exclusion-risk slack. The cutoff, if there is one, depends on how those restrictions affect the sharp bounds for the comorbidity-specific readmission effects.
What exactly should be held fixed in the comparison?

The target should be the same comorbidity-specific 30-day readmission effect, with the same relevant observational information and other stated restrictions. The comparison then asks what changes when physician preference is used as an instrument subject to the allowed exclusion-risk slack, versus the corresponding no-IV analysis. Otherwise, a difference in widths could reflect a change in target or assumptions rather than information from the instrument.
Can we express the stopping condition without pretending to know its value?

Yes. Let the instrument-based bound's width for a given comorbidity stratum be a function of the exclusion-risk slack, and let the corresponding no-IV width be the comparison value. Narrowing occurs when the first width is strictly smaller than the second. A stopping point would be a slack at which that strict inequality no longer holds, if such a point exists in the specified range.
Is equality with the no-IV width the relevant boundary?

Equality marks the loss of a strict width improvement. It is useful to distinguish that boundary from a situation in which the instrument-based width exceeds the no-IV width. The question asks when the bound stops narrowing relative to no-IV; equal widths already answer that in the sense of no longer being narrower.
Would there necessarily be one stopping slack for every comorbidity stratum?

Not necessarily. Different strata could have different comparisons, and the question does not establish that a crossing occurs for any of them. Over a specified slack range, an instrument-based bound might remain narrower, might never be narrower, or might cease to be narrower. Establishing which case applies is part of the proposed analysis.
How should I read the ≤5-point condition: exactly five points, or every first stage up to that size?

It should not be silently replaced with an exactly 5-point first stage. If the question concerns a class of first stages of ≤5 points, you would need to specify whether the requested cutoff is for a particular first stage within that class or is meant to describe all first stages in the class. Those are different claims, and the present question does not resolve the quantifier.
Why does that distinction matter for saying when narrowing stops?

A slack at which narrowing ceases for one allowed first-stage configuration need not be the point at which it ceases for every allowed configuration. A stratum-specific answer for a fixed first stage and a guarantee across the entire ≤5-point class therefore require different comparisons. Neither should be inferred solely from the upper limit of five points.
Does a larger exclusion-risk slack automatically make the instrument-based bound wider?

If increasing slack only relaxes the exclusion restriction while leaving the target and all other constraints fixed, it enlarges the admissible set; under that nesting, a sharp bound cannot become narrower as slack increases. But that conclusion depends on the slack being defined that way. The question itself does not give the formal restriction, so monotonicity should be justified from the eventual formulation rather than assumed from the word “slack.”
Even with that nesting, do we know the width must eventually match no-IV?

No. A nondecreasing instrument-based width need not reach the no-IV width within the slack range under consideration. Whether equality occurs depends on the defined restrictions and the resulting bounds. The threshold could be outside the considered range, or there might be no instrument-based width improvement to lose.
Could the threshold be stated separately for each comorbidity-specific effect?

Yes. That is the most direct reading of comorbidity-specific bounds: compare the instrument-based and no-IV widths for the same effect within each specified stratum. If the aim instead is one slack value at which narrowing stops for all strata, that joint criterion would need to be stated explicitly. No particular comorbidity categories have been specified here.
Does “30-day readmission” affect which widths we compare?

It fixes the outcome and time horizon of the question. Both the instrument-based and no-IV bounds must concern the same comorbidity-specific treatment effect on 30-day readmission. Comparing a bound for a different outcome or horizon would not answer the stated question.
What role does physician preference play in the question?

Physician preference is the proposed instrument whose first stage is constrained to ≤5 points. Its potential contribution is the instrument-based restriction being evaluated against no-IV bounds. The question does not establish that physician preference satisfies exact exclusion, nor does it specify the magnitude of any violation; that is why the comparison varies the permitted exclusion-risk slack.
Could we simply say that a weak first stage makes physician preference unhelpful?

That would prejudge the answer. A ≤5-point first stage signals the weak-instrument setting of this question, but whether physician preference narrows a particular comorbidity-specific bound depends on the other restrictions, including the allowed exclusion-risk slack. The proposed width comparison is needed to determine when it helps and when it stops helping.
Does “exclusion-risk slack” have a numerical unit we can use here?

None is specified. We should retain the term without assigning it an unprovided scale or a numerical value. Before reporting a numerical threshold, the analysis would have to define the slack, its units or parameterization, and the range over which it is varied.
Would a change in an endpoint count as narrowing if the total width stays the same?

Not for the width comparison posed here. An endpoint can move while the width remains unchanged. If the criterion is whether the instrument narrows the bound versus no-IV, the instrument-based width must be strictly smaller than the no-IV width for that same comorbidity-specific effect.
How do the proposed LP bounds help answer this rather than merely give one set of endpoints?

The LP proposal would derive sharp stratified-effect bounds at the relevant exclusion-risk slack values, under the physician-preference first-stage condition being examined. Tracking the resulting widths and comparing them with the corresponding no-IV widths would show whether strict narrowing holds and, if it ceases, where. Sharpness matters because a loose LP bound could make an apparent loss of improvement an artifact of the formulation.
Can I report a slack threshold before establishing sharpness?

You could describe a threshold for whatever bounds you computed, but you could not present it as the point at which the sharp identification bounds stop narrowing unless their sharpness were established. The question concerns the substantive comparison with no-IV bounds, not merely the behavior of an arbitrary relaxation.
Does the uniformly valid 95% weak-IV-robust testing proposal determine the stopping slack?

No. The stopping slack is an identification-bound comparison. Inverting uniformly valid 95% weak-IV-robust moment tests addresses uncertainty in inference under the specified instrument-strength and exclusion-violation classes. The coverage requirement does not, by itself, supply a numerical slack at which the population bounds become as wide as the no-IV bounds.
What is the most precise answer we can give to the question as posed?

The stopping slack is not numerically determinable from the information given. For each specified comorbidity-specific 30-day readmission effect and the intended interpretation of a ≤5-point physician-preference first stage, derive the sharp instrument-based bound as exclusion-risk slack varies and compare its width with the matching no-IV width. The requested point, if it exists, is where strict narrowing ends. State separately if that point differs by stratum or by first-stage configuration, or if no crossing occurs in the specified slack range.

I have a hypothesis for the physician-preference question: with a five-point first stage, exclusion slack under one risk point narrows the comorbidity-specific 30-day readmission bounds, while five points of exclusion slack eliminates the gains over no-IV bounds.

That is a testable hypothesis, not an established threshold. It predicts strict narrowing relative to no-IV bounds when exclusion-risk slack is under one risk point, for a five-point physician-preference first stage. It also predicts no narrowing gain at five points of exclusion slack. It does not say exactly where between those conditions the gain disappears.
Should I describe the first stage as ≤5 points in this hypothesis?

Not without changing its scope. The question concerned a ≤5-point first-stage condition, but this hypothesis specifies a five-point first stage. A finding at exactly five points would not, by itself, establish the same pattern for every smaller first stage.
There are two references to five points. Could they be confused?

Yes, so name them separately: a five-point physician-preference first stage and five points of exclusion-risk slack. The former concerns the strength condition being examined; the latter is the allowed exclusion departure at which the hypothesis predicts no gain over the no-IV bounds. Their equal numerical values do not make them the same quantity.
Does “under one risk point” include exactly one risk point?
No. “Under one risk point” is a strict condition. As worded, the hypothesis does not predict whether narrowing persists, ends, or changes precisely at one risk point of exclusion slack.
And does the five-point claim mean the bounds have to equal the no-IV bounds endpoint for endpoint?

No. “Eliminates no-IV gains” says the proposed instrument-based bounds no longer improve on the no-IV comparison. It does not, on its own, assert that both endpoints coincide. If the gain is evaluated by width, the relevant prediction is that the instrument-based bounds are not strictly narrower at five points of exclusion slack.
Could I say the cutoff is one risk point?

That would overstate the hypothesis. It predicts narrowing below one risk point and no no-IV gain at five points; it leaves the intervening slack values unresolved. In particular, it does not identify one risk point as the slack where narrowing stops.
What if I call five points the cutoff instead?

That would also go beyond the stated claim. Five points of exclusion slack is a condition at which the hypothesis predicts that the gain has been eliminated. The gain might have disappeared earlier; the hypothesis does not locate its first disappearance.
Does this hypothesis apply to an overall treatment effect as well?

It is framed for comorbidity-specific bounds on 30-day readmission effects. It should not be broadened into a claim about an overall effect without a separate statement and comparison for that target.
What comparison would put the hypothesis to the test?

For each specified comorbidity-specific 30-day readmission effect, compare the width of its sharp physician-preference-based bound, under the five-point first stage and each exclusion-risk slack being examined, with the width of its corresponding no-IV bound. The hypothesis predicts strict narrowing for slack under one risk point and no gain over no-IV at five points. The bounds and comparison would have to be established before reporting either prediction as a finding.
Does the hypothesis tell us what happens at every slack between one and five risk points?

No. It gives predictions for slack under one risk point and at five points, but no specific result for the values between them. Even if a formal slack definition supports monotonicity as the restriction is relaxed, the precise point where strict narrowing ends would still have to be determined.
Does it say every comorbidity stratum must lose its gain at the same intermediate slack?

No common intermediate threshold is stated. The hypothesis refers to comorbidity-specific bounds at its stated slack conditions. It does not specify the comorbidity strata or say that any transitions between those conditions occur together.
Could I use the 95% weak-IV-robust confidence sets as evidence that the width prediction is true?

The confidence-set proposal addresses inference and its required coverage; it does not make this identification-bound hypothesis true by itself. The predicted narrowing and loss of no-IV gains concern the sharp bounds. Any uncertainty assessment should be kept distinct from the claim about their widths.
How would you state the hypothesis compactly without making it sound like a result?

Hypothesis: with a five-point physician-preference first stage, exclusion-risk slack under one risk point yields narrower comorbidity-specific 30-day readmission bounds than the corresponding no-IV bounds, whereas five points of exclusion slack eliminates that no-IV width gain. The slack at which narrowing first stops remains to be determined.
How should we plan the analysis of when physician preference stops narrowing the comorbidity-specific 30-day readmission bounds?

Grid physician-preference first-stage values from 0 to 5 points and vary exclusion-risk slack. At each combination, derive the stratified-effect LP bounds and compare their widths with the corresponding no-IV bounds. Separately, invert 95% weak-IV-robust moment tests to construct confidence sets. This is an analysis plan, not a claim about what the grid will show.
Does “0–5-point first stages” mean just the endpoints?

No. It describes the range of first-stage values to examine, including 0 and 5 points and values between them. The plan does not specify grid spacing, so it would be premature to name particular interior values.
Does the same phrase set a 0-to-5-point range for exclusion slack?

No. The stated 0–5-point range applies to first stages. The plan also calls for gridding exclusion slack, but it does not specify that slack's range or spacing. Those choices would need to be stated before carrying out the comparison.
Why vary the first stage instead of looking only at a five-point case?

The question concerns physician-preference first stages of at most 5 points. Examining values across 0–5 points lets the planned comparison address how bound narrowing may depend on the first stage within that range, rather than assuming one value represents them all. It does not predetermine the pattern.
What happens at the zero-point end of the grid?

It is a first-stage value the plan includes. Whether the LP bounds at that value differ from their no-IV counterparts depends on the exact restrictions being used; we should not assign a result before deriving the bounds. Including zero also makes it important that the inference procedure genuinely accommodates weak first stages.
What will the grid produce for each comorbidity stratum?

For each specified stratum and each examined combination of first-stage value and exclusion-risk slack, the planned LP analysis would produce lower and upper bounds for the same comorbidity-specific 30-day readmission effect. Their width can then be compared with the width of that effect's no-IV bound. No particular strata, endpoints, or widths are supplied in the plan.
Why insist on the same effect in the no-IV comparison?

Because the comparison is meant to isolate whether using the instrument narrows a bound. If the instrument-based LP bound and the no-IV bound refer to different strata, outcomes, or time horizons, a difference in width would not answer when physician preference helps for a comorbidity-specific 30-day readmission effect.
How does the plan answer the “stops narrowing” question?

At each examined first-stage value, compare the instrument-based width against its no-IV width as exclusion-risk slack varies. Values where the LP bound is strictly narrower show a width gain on the grid; values where it is not strictly narrower do not. This can locate a change among examined slack values, but a grid alone may not pinpoint an exact stopping slack between them.
Could we report a single stopping value for all first stages from 0 to 5 points?

Only if the comparisons support a clearly defined common criterion. The plan varies the first stage, so it can yield a separate width comparison for each examined value and each specified stratum. It does not assume that all of those comparisons share one stopping slack.
Does an equality of widths count as a gain?

No. If the instrument-based and no-IV widths are equal, the instrument-based bound is not strictly narrower. For this plan's width comparison, narrowing means a smaller LP-bound width than the matching no-IV width.
Why do we need stratified LP bounds rather than one pooled width?

The target is comorbidity-specific effects. A pooled width could obscure what happens in an individual stratum and would not directly answer whether that stratum's bound narrows relative to its no-IV counterpart. The plan therefore compares stratified bounds on a like-for-like basis.
Are the LP calculations intended to be sharp?

That is the identification objective behind the proposal: the LP formulation must yield sharp bounds under the stated restrictions, including the allowed exclusion violations. The grid organizes where those bounds are evaluated; it does not establish sharpness by itself. The formulation would still need to justify that its feasible values match the admissible possibilities.
What does varying exclusion slack change in those LP comparisons?

It changes the permitted exclusion departures according to the restriction eventually specified. The plan asks how the resulting stratified bounds compare with no-IV bounds at the examined slack values. Because the formal slack range and parameterization have not been given, the plan should not assert a numerical stopping point or a numerical rate of widening.
Could the grid itself establish a conclusion for every possible slack and first stage in the range?

Not merely by evaluating finitely many points. A grid directly shows comparisons at its examined combinations. Extending a statement to unexamined values would require an appropriate argument about how the bounds behave between grid points, and the plan does not supply that argument in advance.
Where do the 95% weak-IV-robust moment tests fit in?

They supply the proposed inferential step. For candidate effect values, the plan is to use weak-IV-robust moment tests and invert them, retaining candidates not rejected to form confidence sets. This is distinct from comparing the widths of the population identification bounds.
Does “invert 95% tests” mean that coverage is already guaranteed?

No. The tests must be specified and their error control established. To meet the coverage goal, the resulting confidence sets must have at least 95% coverage uniformly over the specified instrument-strength and exclusion-violation classes. A nominal 95% label or favorable behavior only at the grid points would not establish that uniform guarantee.
Should test inversion be carried out only where the LP bounds beat no-IV?

The plan does not make inference conditional on finding a width gain. Comparing LP widths and inverting weak-IV-robust tests serve different purposes: one assesses when instrument-based identification bounds improve on no-IV, while the other constructs confidence sets with the required coverage. A lack of narrowing at an examined grid point would not remove the need to handle inference correctly if a confidence set is reported there.
Would the test have to reflect exclusion slack as well as first-stage weakness?

Yes, if its confidence set is to address the same allowed configurations as the bounds. The moment-test procedure needs to account for the specified exclusion-violation class and remain valid under the instrument-strength class being considered. Otherwise, the stated uniform 95% coverage goal would not follow from the LP comparison.
Is the inference grid enough to prove uniform coverage across the whole class?

No. Evaluating a procedure on a grid can inform the planned analysis, but uniform coverage is a claim over the specified classes, not just their selected grid points. That claim requires a validity argument for the tests and their inversion across those classes.
Can you state the plan without slipping in a result about where the gain ends?

Examine physician-preference first stages across 0–5 points and a grid of exclusion-risk slack values. For each specified comorbidity-specific 30-day readmission effect, derive the stratified LP bounds at the examined combinations and compare their widths with matching no-IV bounds to investigate when narrowing stops. Invert 95% weak-IV-robust moment tests for confidence sets, with the required uniform coverage to be established rather than assumed. The plan specifies no exclusion-slack cutoff and no observed width or coverage result.
For the simulation activity, I want 10,000 cohorts of 2,000 patients per 0–5-point first-stage/slack cell. We would compare LP versus no-IV widths and 95% weak-IV coverage.

That specifies the replication count and cohort size for each examined combination: 10,000 simulated cohorts, each containing 2,000 patients, per first-stage/slack cell. The comparisons are the stratified LP-bound widths against their matching no-IV widths, and the coverage of the proposed 95% weak-IV-robust confidence procedure. It does not yet state results from those simulations.
Does “per cell” mean 10,000 cohorts for the entire grid?

No. It means 10,000 cohorts for each examined first-stage/slack combination. Each of those cohorts contains 2,000 patients. The total number of simulated cohorts would therefore depend on how many cells the grid contains; the grid spacing and number of slack values have not been specified.
